The compact-type construction in RN100-03 also works over a suitable mixed-characteristic trait: its Jacobian is an abelian scheme although its curve is singular, reflecting the distinction $g=\sum g_\alpha+h_1$ in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 12 (Deligne & Mumford, 1969). A genuinely nonabelian replacement is available for smooth proper curves of genus at least two with a regular semistable model and an integral base point over a complete characteristic-zero DVR with perfect residue field of characteristic $p$: good reduction is equivalent to crystallinity of the unipotent $p$-adic étale fundamental group (Andreatta et al., 2015, Theorems 1.6 and 1.9). matches.text: For the first equality introduced by “Je présume” at the bottom of scan 119, the following derivation **adds** a proof to the analogous tentative normalizer assertion in **LM_140-2_text.tex, scan 84**. Let $F=(L^{\mathrm{sep}})^I=\operatorname{Frac}(V^{\mathrm{sh}})$; it is henselian with value group still $\mathbf Z$, and adjoining an $m$-th root of a uniformizer, for $m>1$ prime to the residue characteristic, shows that $F$ is not separably closed (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tags 0BSW and 0ASF). An element normalizing $I$ preserves $F$ and must preserve its rank-one henselian valuation by the F. K. matches.text: For “ce n'est pas un schéma !” at the end of scan 121, the following argument **adds** a justification and explains the **difference** from the affine-transition construction in **LM_140-4_text.tex, scans 23–24**. Suppose a nonempty open $W$ of the classical Riemann–Zariski space were affine: its quasi-compactness gives $W=p^{-1}(W_0)$ for an open $W_0$ of a suitable normal proper finite-type model (Temkin, 2011, Lemma 3.4.6), and $A=\Gamma(W,\mathcal O)=\Gamma(W_0,\mathcal O)$, since a section is a common rational function and the codimension-one valuation rings on normal $W_0$ force it to be regular there (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 10.157.6, Tag 031T). Choose a closed regular point $a\in W_0$, blow it up, choose two distinct closed points of the exceptional $\mathbf P^{n-1}_{\kappa(a)}$, and choose valuation rings dominating their local rings: they are distinct points of $W$ with the same center $a$, so both induce the same prime $\mathfrak m_a\cap A$, contradicting $W\simeq\operatorname{Spec}A$ (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 10.50.2, Tag 00I8). Confidence: high for $n=\operatorname{trdeg}_K L\geq2$ in this model category, because normality, descent of the quasi-compact open, and distinct centers on the blowup supply the three required steps; this is a proof supplied for the manuscript claim, with no novelty assertion.

Thus contractibility of those strata alone does not recover that full homotopy type, even for an elementary hyperbolic curve; the corresponding local étale inertia also retains procyclic factors. This adds an elementary test to, and agrees with, the circle-fiber data of `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 80 and scans 121–123, while it does not contradict the different nonarchimedean boundary-complex interpretation described by Payne (2013, Remark 1.3). One simplex per nonempty index set produces a single edge, whereas retaining the two components of the intersection gives two edges with common endpoints and hence a circle, as in the component-indexed dual-complex definition (Payne, 2013, §2). This adds a component-counting diagnostic to `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 128–129, whose flag spaces retain component data, and to the componentwise correction on 135. The punctured tube retracts to the Hopf bundle $S^1\to S^3\to S^2$, whose connecting map $\pi_2(S^2)\to\pi_1(S^1)$ is an isomorphism, so the fiber fundamental group is not injected into that tube (Hatcher, 2002, Examples 4.45 and 4.51). This adds an explicit diagnostic to the normal-line-bundle construction and $\pi_2$ warnings in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 122 and 130. A selected geometric inertia conjugacy class is stabilized by $G_{\mathbf Q(\sqrt2)}$, whereas the pair is $G_{\mathbf Q}$-equivariant; distinct cusp classes are not identified by geometric conjugation (Stix, 2012, Proposition 16). This adds a concrete scope test and agrees with the rational-boundary restriction and finite-base-change discussion in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 83–84. | BISITE D.2 | A complete realization theorem for finite Alexandrov bases. Let $P$ be a finite poset with the topology of downsets. There are equivalences \[ (\mathrm{Top}/P)[(W^{\mathrm{opn}}_P)^{-1}] \simeq\operatorname{Fun}(P,\mathcal S) \simeq\operatorname{CoShv}(P;\mathcal S). \tag{D.2} \] The first equivalence sends $f:X\to P$ to the covariant diagram $p\mapsto\Pi f^{-1}(P_{\leq p})$. matches.text: | BISITE D.6 | Proper base change is a coefficient theorem. Consider a cartesian square of locally compact Hausdorff spaces \[ \begin{array}{ccc} X'&\xrightarrow{g'}&X\\[-2pt] {\scriptstyle f'}\downarrow&&\downarrow{\scriptstyle f}\\[-2pt] Y'&\xrightarrow{g}&Y. \end{array} \] If $f$ is proper, the canonical mate $g^*f_*\to f'_*g'^*$ is an equivalence on sheaves of spaces. It is also an equivalence on sheaves with values in a stable bicomplete infinity-category. These are ordinary infinity-sheaves; hypercompletion is not silently substituted. | claim (return: Known) | Unverified citation (HTT 7.3.1.18; Volpe). |

matches.text: | BISITE D.7 | A precise smooth topological comparison. A space $K$ is essential when the constant-sheaf functor $\mathcal S\to\operatorname{Shv}(K;\mathcal S)$ has a left adjoint. A shape submersion $g:Z\to Y$ is locally, on its source, a projection $V\times K\to V$ with $V$ open in $Y$ and $K$ essential. Assume either $Y$ is locally compact or all these $K$ are locally compact. Then for any presentable coefficient infinity-category $\mathcal C$ there is an adjunction $g_\sharp\dashv g^*$ on sheaves with these coefficients. In a cartesian square as in D.6 with $g$ a shape submersion and with the same local compactness condition after pullback, the canonical maps \[ g'_\sharp f'^*\longrightarrow f^*g_\sharp, \qquad g^*f_*\longrightarrow f'_*g'^* \] are equivalences. | claim (return: Known) | Unverified citation (Volpe 2025, 3.23–3.27). |

matches.text: | BISITE D.8 | The stable sheaf--cosheaf equivalence and the shriek operation. For a locally compact Hausdorff space $Y$ and a stable bicomplete infinity-category $\mathcal C$, there is an equivalence \[ \mathbb V_Y:\operatorname{Shv}(Y;\mathcal C) \xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }\operatorname{CoShv}(Y;\mathcal C), \qquad \mathbb V_Y(F)(U)= \operatorname*{colim}_{K\subseteq U\ { m compact}} \operatorname{fib}\bigl(F(Y)\to F(Y\setminus K)\bigr). \tag{D.8} \] For a continuous map $f:X\to Y$ between such spaces, cosheaf pushforward $f_+$ is $(f_+G)(U)=G(f^{-1}U)$. The topological operation with proper support is $f_!=\mathbb V_Y^{-1}f_+\mathbb V_X$ and has a right adjoint $f^!$. For proper $f$ it agrees with $f_*$. This does not identify $f_!$ with the left adjoint $f_\sharp$ of D.7. | claim (return: Known) | Unverified citation (HA 5.5.5.1; Volpe 6.9). |

matches.text: | BISITE D.11 | The realization comparison for every proper map of finite posets. Let $f:P\to Q$ be a $W_\infty$-proper map of finite posets. Equivalently, for every $p\in P$ and $q\geq f(p)$ the outgoing lifting poset \[ L(p,q)=\{r\in P:r\geq p,\ f(r)=q\} \tag{D.11a} \] is weakly contractible. This holds for spaces, spectra, and the derived category of modules over any ring. matches.text: | BISITE D.13 | A specified stable cosheaf counterpart for smooth finite-poset maps. There is a precise geometric dual on finite coefficients which uses the maximum stratification and Verdier transport. Let $\mathcal C$ be spectra or modules over a commutative ring, let $D$ be the coefficient duality on finite spectra or perfect modules, and let $E_P^{\max}:\operatorname{Fun}(P,\mathcal C)\to \operatorname{Shv}(\|NP\|;\mathcal C)$ be G.10 for $P^{\mathrm{op}}$. Define the contravariant fully faithful functor \[ \Phi_P(F)=\mathbb V_{\|NP\|}\,E_P^{\max}(DF), \qquad F\in\operatorname{Fun}(P^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal C^{\mathrm{perf}}). \tag{D.13a} \] If $f:P\to Q$ is categorically smooth, then its realization $g$ satisfies \[ \Phi_Q(f_!F)\simeq g_+\Phi_P(F). \tag{D.13b} \] Thus ordinary cosheaf pushforward realizes this specified dual of left Kan extension. The cosheaf subcategories in (D.13a) are defined as Verdier images of maximum-constructible perfect sheaves; they are not being identified with literal minimum-constructible cosheaves. For a noncommutative ring the target coefficients are modules over its opposite ring. | claim (return: Proved) | Unverified. |

matches.text: The assertion that “$D=S\setminus S^{\prime}$ est purement de codim $1$” follows if the rational map extends to the compactification and the pulled-back boundary equation remains a non-zero-divisor. In that situation the inverse image is an effective Cartier divisor, hence has pure codimension one; the local pullback condition is essential (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tag 01WQ). This adds a global divisor interpretation to the “indice de ramification” discussed in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 45. The parenthesis about $g\geq1$ or a one-dimensional base should therefore be kept as part of the author’s extension argument, rather than treating purity as a property of every indeterminacy locus on an arbitrary higher-dimensional base.

matches.text: The qualification “de façon ess. canonique” is naturally read at the level of a conjugacy class of peripheral subgroups, since a chosen geometric path is needed to place a particular $L_i$ inside a fixed based $\pi$. This restates the peripheral intersection $\mathcal E_i\cap\pi=L_i$ in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 53, while scan 69 adds the stronger transporter-reconstruction question. For hyperbolic curves in the relevant arithmetic setting, the peripheral decomposition subgroup is recovered as the normalizer of inertia (Tamagawa, 1997, Remark 7.5). That result explains the normalizer appearing here and on scan 099, but does not make every choice of a representative subgroup or of a cusp splitting canonical.

matches.text: The desired “vue d’ensemble” can be organized by composing group homomorphisms over the arithmetic quotient, with residue-field maps supplied by decomposition groups rather than by nonexistent canonical inclusions $k(s)\subset K$. This adds a comparison between the local groupoid in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 26, and the conjugacy classification of splittings on scan 63 (“mod. autom. intérieurs”). For a fixed based extension, a splitting gives an actual conjugation action on its geometric kernel, whereas changing the base point or transport path changes the comparison by an inner automorphism. The latter dependence is explicit in SGA 1, Exposé XIII, §2.10, and explains why the author’s insistence on “effectives” requires compatible choices (Grothendieck, 1971/2003).

matches.text: The margin “dans le contexte des VA” plausibly alludes to the abelian-variety good-reduction criterion, but neither the abbreviation nor this autobiographical claim identifies a particular publication. Its terminology restates the use of “V.A.” and $\pi_{\mathrm{ab}}$ in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 64, but that passage concerns recognizing points and does not establish a curve-reduction theorem. The Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich–Serre–Tate criterion detects good reduction of an abelian variety from its prime-to-residue-characteristic Tate module; the precise statement was checked in Andreatta et al. (2015, Theorem 1.1), with Serre and Tate (1968) retained as the original bibliographic reference. For a proper curve this controls its Jacobian, and the compact-type example below prevents transferring the criterion to the curve itself.

matches.text: The expectation “être connu sur $H_1$” invites the following editorial counterexample: join two elliptic curves over $\mathbf Q$ at rational points and smooth their single node over $\mathbf Q[[t]]$, locally by $xy=t$. This adds a reduction test to `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 12, whose formula $g=\sum g_\alpha+h_1$ separates the component genera from cycles in the dual graph. The graph is a tree, so the degree-zero Picard scheme has no toric part and the Jacobian has good reduction, whereas uniqueness of the stable model leaves the genus-two curve with its singular special fiber; its inertia on $H_1$ is therefore trivial despite bad curve reduction (Deligne & Mumford, 1969, Proposition 1.5, Theorem 1.11, Lemma 1.17, and Theorem 2.5; Grothendieck, 1971/2003, Exposé X, Corollary 3.9). Confidence is high because independent node smoothing, the graph–torus computation, and stable-model uniqueness give each step; removing one section through a smooth rational point leaves $H_1$ unchanged and gives an affine hyperbolic counterexample as well.

matches.text: At scan 105, manuscript page 52, (2) defines the precise group by $\pi_1(X;\widetilde X)=\operatorname{Aut}_X(\widetilde X)$. This **restates** the representing-cover viewpoint in **LM_140-2_text.tex, scans 8–10**, where the covariant fibre functor is $T\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}(S,T)$, but those passages do not explicitly settle the left/right convention in the present formula. Precomposition on $F(W)=\operatorname{Hom}_X(\widetilde X,W)$ reverses composition, so it identifies $\operatorname{Aut}_X(\widetilde X)^{\mathrm{op}}$ with $\operatorname{Aut}(F)$; using the inverse deck transformation instead gives a left action, exactly the convention issue made explicit in the proof of Lemma 58.3.9 (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tag 0BMQ). matches.text: The reference to $\mathfrak m_{s_\alpha}/\mathfrak m_{s_\alpha}^{2}$ and the « faisceau conormal » suggests tracing a chosen first-order parameter through the normal-torus construction used for higher-codimension boundary strata. **Context comparison — adds a link:** `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 73–75, treats Kummer torsors of tangential splittings, whereas `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 122–123, constructs punctured **normal** line bundles and their product torsors; the conormal line on scan 95 is their dual in the Cartier-divisor situation. A useful check is to compute the effect of $t\mapsto ut$ on the associated splitting class and to track the duality when comparing Chern classes, rather than identifying the two torsor conventions by notation alone (Talpo & Vistoli, 2018, §3, supplies a modern divisor-root framework). **Our confidence: medium**, because the first-order and line-bundle data are visibly present in both manuscripts, but a full identification must specify the parameter, basepoint, and duality conventions.

matches.text: | RESIDUE H.7 | The program \path{code/GHIJ/finite_poset_direct_image.py} independently enumerates all maps between one representative of every poset isomorphism class with at most five objects, including the empty poset. The counts of posets of sizes $0,1,2,3,4,5$ are $1,1,2,5,16,63$. It examines $1,349,916$ monotone maps and recognizes $96,372$ proper maps. Properness is certified by explicit simplicial collapses of every nonempty outgoing lifting order complex; noncontractible cases are rejected by homology over $\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb F_2$. The program aborts rather than classifying an acyclic but uncertified complex as contractible. No such undecided case occurs in this range. For every proper map and every nonempty target simplex, it computes the categorical stalk and the actual geometric-fibre cellular cohomology, for the constant coefficient and for each principal-cosieve indicator. This gives $5,536,094$ stalk/coefficient cases, each computed over both $\mathbb Q$ and $\mathbb F_2$, with no discrepancy. A fibre cell is indexed by a source chain meeting each level of the target simplex; it is a product of simplices, of dimension $\|\kappa\|-\|\sigma\|$. Its signed boundary deletes one vertex while keeping every level nonempty, using the product-boundary sign. The code verifies that consecutive boundary matrices multiply to zero. Exact rational ranks use integer elimination with gcd reduction, and binary ranks use bit arithmetic. For a principal cosieve, extension from the corresponding closed subcomplex reduces both computations to its intersection with the relevant fibre or lower inverse image. The supplied per-map CSV records all tests as successful; the JSON gives the totals by source and target size. These numerical comparisons check cohomology, not a replacement proof of the canonical mate; the latter is established in H.1. | claim (return: Proved) | no review |

matches.text: The qualified assertion about “l’ens des pts fermés” is valid as a uniqueness statement for already existing morphisms from a reduced finite-type scheme over a field to a separated target, provided their restrictions as morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)\to Y$ agree, including the residue-field maps. Indeed, the equalizer is closed and contains every closed point, so density and reducedness force equality as morphisms; finite-type schemes over fields are Jacobson (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tag 01T9). The present passage adds this specialization family to `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 63 (“classes de scindages”), while scan 64 already marks the unrestricted point–section bijection “faux tel quel”. Recovering a rational section from an arbitrary compatible family of abstract group splittings is a stronger existence problem and does not follow from closed-point density.

matches.text: The question “Et que se passe-t-il pour $s\notin S^{\prime}$ ?” suggests an editorial calculation at a regular point where the exceptional divisor has simple normal crossings. This adds local section data to the branch bookkeeping in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 107, rather than assuming that a single rank-one inertia group captures every branch. If a boundary parameter pulls back as $u\prod_{j=1}^{r}t_j^{m_j}$, Kummer theory sends the $j$th tame inertia generator to $m_j$ times the target generator, while the unit supplies the residual Kummer class (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tag 03PK). Confidence is high for this explicit local calculation, but its globalization needs additional choices; Deligne’s higher-dimensional discussion in §15.2 is itself a proposed framework, whereas his subsequent detailed construction treats curves (Deligne, 1989).

This explains the stated open locus without extending the conclusion across zeros, poles, or singularities of the divisor.

matches.text: The desired “vue d’ensemble” can be organized by composing group homomorphisms over the arithmetic quotient, with residue-field maps supplied by decomposition groups rather than by nonexistent canonical inclusions $k(s)\subset K$. This adds a comparison between the local groupoid in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 26, and the conjugacy classification of splittings on scan 63 (“mod. autom. intérieurs”). For a fixed based extension, a splitting gives an actual conjugation action on its geometric kernel, whereas changing the base point or transport path changes the comparison by an inner automorphism. The latter dependence is explicit in SGA 1, Exposé XIII, §2.10, and explains why the author’s insistence on “effectives” requires compatible choices (Grothendieck, 1971/2003).

matches.text: The conjecture “ssi il y a bonne réduction” has a precise later theorem for hyperbolic pointed curves over a discrete valuation field. Tamagawa proves that good reduction of the pair is equivalent to trivial outer inertia on one, equivalently every, prime-to-residue-characteristic pro-$\ell$ geometric fundamental group (Tamagawa, 1997, Theorem 5.3). This adds a group criterion to the marked-curve setting of `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 5, with its “fini étale” boundary. In the manuscript’s residue-characteristic-zero situation, this validates the nonabelian a)–b) comparison, without validating the proposed substitutions of $H_1$ in c) and d).

matches.text: The margin “dans le contexte des VA” plausibly alludes to the abelian-variety good-reduction criterion, but neither the abbreviation nor this autobiographical claim identifies a particular publication. Its terminology restates the use of “V.A.” and $\pi_{\mathrm{ab}}$ in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 64, but that passage concerns recognizing points and does not establish a curve-reduction theorem. The Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich–Serre–Tate criterion detects good reduction of an abelian variety from its prime-to-residue-characteristic Tate module; the precise statement was checked in Andreatta et al. (2015, Theorem 1.1), with Serre and Tate (1968) retained as the original bibliographic reference. For a proper curve this controls its Jacobian, and the compact-type example below prevents transferring the criterion to the curve itself.

matches.text: The expectation “être connu sur $H_1$” invites the following editorial counterexample: join two elliptic curves over $\mathbf Q$ at rational points and smooth their single node over $\mathbf Q[[t]]$, locally by $xy=t$. This adds a reduction test to `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 12, whose formula $g=\sum g_\alpha+h_1$ separates the component genera from cycles in the dual graph. The graph is a tree, so the degree-zero Picard scheme has no toric part and the Jacobian has good reduction, whereas uniqueness of the stable model leaves the genus-two curve with its singular special fiber; its inertia on $H_1$ is therefore trivial despite bad curve reduction (Deligne & Mumford, 1969, Proposition 1.5, Theorem 1.11, Lemma 1.17, and Theorem 2.5; Grothendieck, 1971/2003, Exposé X, Corollary 3.9). Confidence is high because independent node smoothing, the graph–torus computation, and stable-model uniqueness give each step; removing one section through a smooth rational point leaves $H_1$ unchanged and gives an affine hyperbolic counterexample as well.

matches.text: The question “qu’attendre d’une telle action ?” can first be separated into its formal and geometric parts. It restates the splitting framework of `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 63, while scan 413 adds an independent admissibility condition for actual lifts. After fixing one section $s$, another has the form $s^{\prime}(g)=c(g)s(g)$ with $c$ a continuous nonabelian $1$-cocycle in $\pi$, and its action is $\operatorname{Int}(c(g))\alpha_s(g)$. Thus changing the section of (31) preserves the outer action but can change the actual action and its point-theoretic interpretation; this is a direct calculation from multiplication in the extension.

This restates the “maquette” in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 11, and adds an arithmetic question to the three boundary partitions of the four-pointed line on scan 61. Independent node-smoothing parameters give local boundary directions, while the graph distinguishes a separating node from a loop contributing to the Jacobian’s toric part (Deligne & Mumford, 1969, Proposition 1.5 and Lemma 1.17). Consequently the graph supplies useful test cases for the conjectural equivalences without itself determining the entire arithmetic outer action.

matches.text: The suggestion of a criterion “sur les groupes $p$-divisibles” is appropriate to abelian-variety data, but the Jacobian’s Barsotti–Tate group alone cannot detect every node of the curve. The compact-type construction in RN100-03 also works over a suitable mixed-characteristic trait: its Jacobian is an abelian scheme although its curve is singular, reflecting the distinction $g=\sum g_\alpha+h_1$ in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 12 (Deligne & Mumford, 1969). A genuinely nonabelian replacement is available for smooth proper curves of genus at least two with a regular semistable model and an integral base point over a complete characteristic-zero DVR with perfect residue field of characteristic $p$: good reduction is equivalent to crystallinity of the unipotent $p$-adic étale fundamental group (Andreatta et al., 2015, Theorems 1.6 and 1.9). This differs from testing only the Jacobian’s $p$-divisible group and should remain separate from the prime-to-$p$ outer-inertia criterion.

matches.text: The invitation “Le cas du genre $0$” has an explicit editorial test: $U=\mathbf P^1_{\mathbf Q((t))}\setminus\{0,t,1,\infty\}$ has all four punctures rational and $H_1(U_{\bar K},\mathbf Z_\ell)\simeq\mathbf Z_\ell(1)^3$, so its $t$-adic inertia acts trivially for every $\ell$ (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tag 03PK). This adds the family deferred by “Je vais pas le faire ici” in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 62, to the cross-ratio description on scan 61. The cross-ratio $t$ meets the boundary, and blowing up the collision of $0$ and $t$ produces two rational components with two marked points and a node on each, so the pointed curve has bad reduction although its compactification is smooth. Confidence is high because the boundary collision and Kummer homology are explicit; only the local $t$-adic inertia is trivial on $H_1$, while the full arithmetic action still contains the cyclotomic character.

matches.text: For “Ladite extension est admissible” on scan 102, the counterexample to e)$\Rightarrow$a) survives the stronger quantifier “for every splitting”: for any section $s:G_{\mathbf Q}\to G_K$, the restricted descent cocycle is the continuous quadratic character $\chi_t\circ s$. Kummer theory realizes it by a quadratic twist $U_0^{(d)}/\mathbf Q$, so the full pulled-back outer action, and hence its center-free-kernel extension, is geometric; the fixed point $(0,0)$ also supplies the corresponding geometric actual lift (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tag 03PK; Tamagawa, 1997, Lemma 7.1). This contradicts the proposed implication even with the splitting quantifier strengthened, while restating the “réalisable” interpretation in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 410, and adding an explicit calculation to the splitting classes on scan 63. Confidence is high because the argument restricts the actual geometric descent cocycle before applying fundamental groups, rather than inferring full geometricity from $H_1$.

In RN103-01, all punctures are rational and their boundary permutation module is constant, yet their closures collide; the abelianized representation consequently loses the cross-ratio degeneration. The proposed genus-zero investigation therefore isolates precisely why a boundary permutation representation, even together with the compactification’s homology, need not recover good reduction of the pointed curve.

matches.text: At scan 105, manuscript page 52, (2) defines the precise group by $\pi_1(X;\widetilde X)=\operatorname{Aut}_X(\widetilde X)$. This **restates** the representing-cover viewpoint in **LM_140-2_text.tex, scans 8–10**, where the covariant fibre functor is $T\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}(S,T)$, but those passages do not explicitly settle the left/right convention in the present formula. The Artin–Schreier cover $z^p-z=tx$ of $X_T$ gives a class in $\Omega[x]/\{h^p-h\}$ outside the image of $k[x]/\{h^p-h\}$, so the natural $\pi_1(X_T)\to\pi_1(X)$ cannot be an isomorphism although $T$ is $1$-connected (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tag 0A3J; compare the same obstruction in Landesman, 2024, Example 1.7). This **differs** from the characteristic-zero curve setting of **LM_140-2_text.tex, scans 19–22**, and does not affect scan 106's change of the field of a base point while keeping $X$ fixed. Confidence: high, because polynomial Artin–Schreier classes detect the failure explicitly; this is an application of a known obstruction to the manuscript's wording, not a claim of a new counterexample in the literature.

A precise finite case is the Stein factorization of a proper flat finitely presented map with geometrically reduced fibres, for which $Y'\to Y$ is finite étale (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 58.15.1, Tag 0BUN); the closed image of $\pi_1(X)\to\pi_1(Y)$ instead determines a pointed profinite cover in Galois theory, without automatically being an open subgroup or a finite cover. matches.text: For “ce n'est pas un schéma !” at the end of scan 121, the following argument **adds** a justification and explains the **difference** from the affine-transition construction in **LM_140-4_text.tex, scans 23–24**. Suppose a nonempty open $W$ of the classical Riemann–Zariski space were affine: its quasi-compactness gives $W=p^{-1}(W_0)$ for an open $W_0$ of a suitable normal proper finite-type model (Temkin, 2011, Lemma 3.4.6), and $A=\Gamma(W,\mathcal O)=\Gamma(W_0,\mathcal O)$, since a section is a common rational function and the codimension-one valuation rings on normal $W_0$ force it to be regular there (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 10.157.6, Tag 031T). Choose a closed regular point $a\in W_0$, blow it up, choose two distinct closed points of the exceptional $\mathbf P^{n-1}_{\kappa(a)}$, and choose valuation rings dominating their local rings: they are distinct points of $W$ with the same center $a$, so both induce the same prime $\mathfrak m_a\cap A$, contradicting $W\simeq\operatorname{Spec}A$ (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 10.50.2, Tag 00I8). Confidence: high for $n=\operatorname{trdeg}_K L\geq2$ in this model category, because normality, descent of the quasi-compact open, and distinct centers on the blowup supply the three required steps; this is a proof supplied for the manuscript claim, with no novelty assertion.

matches.text: At scan 122, the opening continuation of scan 121 says that codimension-one points “correspondent exactement” to the indicated finite-type “jauges”, with “ess.” versus “ext.” still marked as a reading doubt. With the manuscript's codimension $n-\operatorname{trdeg}_K\kappa(V)$, lift $n-1$ algebraically independent residue elements to $V$ and choose a normal proper model where those lifts are regular at its center: the center has codimension one, its local ring is a DVR dominated by $V$, and hence equals $V$, giving an essentially finite-type divisorial valuation ring. This **adds** the higher-dimensional residue criterion to the curve-local “anneau-jauge” in **LM_140-2_text.tex, scan 25**, and agrees with the description of Zariski prime divisors by codimension-one local rings and residue transcendence degree in Pop (2006, pp. 294–295). Confidence: high in the divisorial characterization, including the converse supplied by a prime divisor on a normal model; it neither identifies all discrete valuations with divisorial ones nor resolves the abbreviated handwritten adjective.

matches.text: For the boundary-index convention $J\ne\varnothing$ and the complex punctured-tube realization, take $U=\mathbf P^1\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}$: all nonempty boundary strata are points, the maquette is three isolated vertices, and the punctured tube retracts onto three circles. Thus contractibility of those strata alone does not recover that full homotopy type, even for an elementary hyperbolic curve; the corresponding local étale inertia also retains procyclic factors. This adds an elementary test to, and agrees with, the circle-fiber data of `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 80 and scans 121–123, while it does not contradict the different nonarchimedean boundary-complex interpretation described by Payne (2013, Remark 1.3). matches.text: Defining the fundamental groupoids “par revêtements et isomorphismes entre tels” requires a decision about which coverings are retained. The passage restates the covering-category approach of `LM_140-4_text.tex`, scans 246–249, and the multigaloisian reconstruction of `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 7–8; those passages discuss universal coverings and ordinary groups, whereas SGA 1's Galois categories use finite coverings and profinite groups (Grothendieck & Raynaud, 2003, Exposé V, §5). A comparison must therefore state whether it concerns all topological coverings, finite coverings, or a completion, and must not silently replace the manuscript's discrete lattice kernels by profinite lattices.

For a finite group acting smoothly on a paracompact manifold and preserving a closed embedded submanifold, averaging a Riemannian metric supplies an invariant metric, whose normal exponential map gives an equivariant tubular neighborhood after restricting its domain; this is a concrete mechanism absent for the displayed infinite transvection action. The proposal adds a conditional repair to the quotient-germ programme of `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 78–80, and to the equivariance comparisons in `LM_140-4_text.tex`, scans 263–264; confidence is high for the metric construction under the stated hypotheses, but it does not establish descent for arbitrary multiplicities or simultaneous compatibility with every boundary branch.

This **adds** a selection of whole normalized branches to the branch-intersection construction in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 106 and 108, rather than simply pulling back a closed subset. For two transverse branches with $\Sigma$ equal to one branch, the full inverse image in $D_1$ also contains the intersection point on the other normalized branch, whereas the revised definition selects only the component lying wholly in $\Sigma$. The assertion that these component selections recover every admissible $\Sigma$ needs the local branch model and the fact that the selected images form the required closed union.

matches.text: The claim that the “donnée … est équivalente” to compatible subsets of $\pi_0(D_d)$ makes the admissible closed $\Sigma$ recoverable from the global component data rather than arbitrary local labels. The count is interpreted in the planar model as the centre, three rays, and three sectors; it does not by itself disprove the Segal identity, finite étaleness, or any particular homotopy-reconstruction assertion. A useful axiomatization should therefore keep the Boolean local-order condition separate from the categorical and topological conditions.

The qualified assertion about “l’ens des pts fermés” is valid as a uniqueness statement for already existing morphisms from a reduced finite-type scheme over a field to a separated target, provided their restrictions as morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)\to Y$ agree, including the residue-field maps. Indeed, the equalizer is closed and contains every closed point, so density and reducedness force equality as morphisms; finite-type schemes over fields are Jacobson (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tag 01T9). The present passage adds this specialization family to `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 63 (“classes de scindages”), while scan 64 already marks the unrestricted point–section bijection “faux tel quel”. Recovering a rational section from an arbitrary compatible family of abstract group splittings is a stronger existence problem and does not follow from closed-point density.

matches.text: The question “comment voir que e) implique bonne réduction” has a counterexample in its stated generality: over $K=\mathbf Q((t))$, let $E_t:y^2=x^3-t^2x$ and $U_t=E_t\setminus\{O\}$, the ramified quadratic twist of $U_0$ for $E_0:y^2=x^3-x$. The isomorphism $(X,Y)\mapsto(tX,t^{3/2}Y)$ over $K(\sqrt t)$ has descent cocycle $[-1]$, so inertia acts as $-1$ on $H_1$ and rules out good reduction, whereas the uniformizer-based residue splitting fixing $\sqrt t$ pulls the full outer action back to that of $U_0/\mathbf Q$ (Grothendieck, 1971/2003, Exposé X, Corollary 3.9; The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tag 03PK). The current passage adds a reduction implication to the realization meaning in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 410; this example disproves that addition using the local splitting construction of scan 75. Confidence is high because the coordinate change and descent cocycle are explicit; this is an editorial counterexample with finite nontrivial inertia, and no extra semistability assumption is being inserted into the manuscript.

matches.text: The tentative “ne soient géométriques” does hold for the editorial test $U=E_q\setminus\{O\}$ over $\mathbf Q((q))$: after any splitting $G_{\mathbf Q}\to G_K$, the Tate-module semisimplification is $\mathbf Q_\ell(1)\oplus\mathbf Q_\ell$, by Tate’s exact torsion sequence (Tate, 1995, manuscript p. 19). This adds a concrete use of the “non-trivialité à la Weil” proposed in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 85. The weight-zero constituent persists after every finite number-field extension, whereas a hypothetical realizing smooth curve has, at a suitable good finite prime, $H^1$ of weights at least one and therefore no weight-zero constituent in its dual $H_1$ (Deligne, 1980, Corollary 3.3.5). Confidence is high because the obstruction uses only the invariant subquotients and their weights; it proves nongeometricity in this Tate case, without reversing the quadratic-twist counterexample or asserting a universal bad-reduction principle.

This **adds** a larger separably closed field of a base point to **LM_140-2_text.tex, scan 22**, which describes a separable residue-field closure, and scan 108 of the present manuscript itself explicitly says “clôtures séparables dans $\Omega$”. Finite étale residue extensions factor through the separable algebraic closure inside $\Omega$, giving the fibre-functor comparison for the fixed scheme $X$ (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 58.6.3, Tag 0BQ8), but a merely separably closed $\Omega$ need not contain an algebraic closure in the purely inseparable sense. matches.text: At scan 115, manuscript page 57, the final paragraph says that the quotient of $\mathcal E_L^{\overline L}$ “ne … dépend pas du modèle $X$ choisi”, for $X$ proper and regular. This **adds** a birationally invariant quotient to the local curve-boundary construction in **LM_140-2_text.tex, scans 25–28**. Given two such models, a finite étale cover of one is unramified at every $K$-valuation by the valuative criterion of properness, hence at the codimension-one local rings of the other, and its finite normalization over the other is étale by regular-target purity; thus the quotient of the fixed $G_L$, not merely its abstract isomorphism type, agrees (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tags 0BQJ and 0BMB). Confidence: high when the proper regular models exist; this comparison does not itself prove their existence or require a general resolution theorem to compare two already given models.

matches.text: For “A t-on une réciproque ?” on scan 120, take $K=\mathbf C$, $L=\mathbf C(t)$, $U=\mathbf A^1_{\mathbf C}$, and the valuation at infinity on $\mathbf P^1_{\mathbf C}$. Its nontrivial inertia maps trivially to $\pi_1(U)=1$, since the complex affine line is simply connected and the étale group is its profinite completion, but the unique center of the valuation on the proper model is $\infty\notin U$ (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Section 64.27, “Comparison,” Tag 03VD, and Lemma 58.13.5, Tag 0BUA). This **differs** from the restricted curve classes in **LM_140-2_text.tex, scan 20**, and is permitted by scan 115's explicit allowance for algebraically closed $K$. Confidence: high because both the trivial target group and the missing center are explicit; the example does not disprove the additional marginal restriction, and the same test can be transferred to $\mathbf A^1_{\mathbf Q}$ using characteristic-zero base-change invariance and the arithmetic sequence (Landesman, 2024, Theorem 1.1; The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tag 0BTX).

matches.text: The NB beside (31) on scan 121, manuscript page 60, says “Cette définition ne dépend pas de l'hypothèse de résolution des sing” because normal proper models may replace regular ones. This agrees with the modern Riemann–Zariski construction as a locally ringed inverse limit over proper birational models; normal models suffice, and regular models give the same limit when a resolution theorem supplies a cofinal family of them (Temkin, 2011, Introduction and Proposition 2.2.1). It **differs** from **LM_140-4_text.tex, scans 23–24**, whose projective system of group schemes is representable as a scheme because its transition maps are affine, a condition not supplied for the proper birational transitions here. Confidence: high in the resolution-independent normal-model construction and in the conditional cofinality statement; no unrestricted resolution theorem is being assumed.

For a finitely generated field extension $L/K$, the zero-dimensional space is $\operatorname{Spec}L$, and in transcendence degree one the normal proper curve already represents the valuation space; in higher transcendence degree, 121-O1 supplies a separate obstruction to any affine open neighborhood. This **differs** from the affine-transition limit in **LM_140-4_text.tex, scans 23–24**, and is compatible with Olberding's criterion relating affine subspaces of a Zariski–Riemann space to Prüfer intersection rings (Olberding, 2015, Proposition 6.1; preprint Theorem 6.1). Confidence: high under this normal finite-type model interpretation; neither the mere existence of nonnoetherian stalks nor the incorrect noetherian-stalk assertion assessed in 122-CJ1 would prove nonschematicity.

matches.text: For “ce n'est pas un schéma !” at the end of scan 121, the following argument **adds** a justification and explains the **difference** from the affine-transition construction in **LM_140-4_text.tex, scans 23–24**. Suppose a nonempty open $W$ of the classical Riemann–Zariski space were affine: its quasi-compactness gives $W=p^{-1}(W_0)$ for an open $W_0$ of a suitable normal proper finite-type model (Temkin, 2011, Lemma 3.4.6), and $A=\Gamma(W,\mathcal O)=\Gamma(W_0,\mathcal O)$, since a section is a common rational function and the codimension-one valuation rings on normal $W_0$ force it to be regular there (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 10.157.6, Tag 031T). Choose a closed regular point $a\in W_0$, blow it up, choose two distinct closed points of the exceptional $\mathbf P^{n-1}_{\kappa(a)}$, and choose valuation rings dominating their local rings: they are distinct points of $W$ with the same center $a$, so both induce the same prime $\mathfrak m_a\cap A$, contradicting $W\simeq\operatorname{Spec}A$ (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 10.50.2, Tag 00I8). Confidence: high for $n=\operatorname{trdeg}_K L\geq2$ in this model category, because normality, descent of the quasi-compact open, and distinct centers on the blowup supply the three required steps; this is a proof supplied for the manuscript claim, with no novelty assertion.

matches.text: At scan 122, the opening continuation of scan 121 says that codimension-one points “correspondent exactement” to the indicated finite-type “jauges”, with “ess.” versus “ext.” still marked as a reading doubt. With the manuscript's codimension $n-\operatorname{trdeg}_K\kappa(V)$, lift $n-1$ algebraically independent residue elements to $V$ and choose a normal proper model where those lifts are regular at its center: the center has codimension one, its local ring is a DVR dominated by $V$, and hence equals $V$, giving an essentially finite-type divisorial valuation ring. This **adds** the higher-dimensional residue criterion to the curve-local “anneau-jauge” in **LM_140-2_text.tex, scan 25**, and agrees with the description of Zariski prime divisors by codimension-one local rings and residue transcendence degree in Pop (2006, pp. 294–295). Confidence: high in the divisorial characterization, including the converse supplied by a prime divisor on a normal model; it neither identifies all discrete valuations with divisorial ones nor resolves the abbreviated handwritten adjective.

matches.text: | BISITE D.7 | A precise smooth topological comparison. A space $K$ is essential when the constant-sheaf functor $\mathcal S\to\operatorname{Shv}(K;\mathcal S)$ has a left adjoint. A shape submersion $g:Z\to Y$ is locally, on its source, a projection $V\times K\to V$ with $V$ open in $Y$ and $K$ essential. Assume either $Y$ is locally compact or all these $K$ are locally compact. Then for any presentable coefficient infinity-category $\mathcal C$ there is an adjunction $g_\sharp\dashv g^*$ on sheaves with these coefficients. In a cartesian square as in D.6 with $g$ a shape submersion and with the same local compactness condition after pullback, the canonical maps \[ g'_\sharp f'^*\longrightarrow f^*g_\sharp, \qquad g^*f_*\longrightarrow f'_*g'^* \] are equivalences. | claim (return: Known) | Unverified citation (Volpe 2025, 3.23–3.27). |

matches.text: | BISITE D.8 | The stable sheaf--cosheaf equivalence and the shriek operation. For a locally compact Hausdorff space $Y$ and a stable bicomplete infinity-category $\mathcal C$, there is an equivalence \[ \mathbb V_Y:\operatorname{Shv}(Y;\mathcal C) \xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }\operatorname{CoShv}(Y;\mathcal C), \qquad \mathbb V_Y(F)(U)= \operatorname*{colim}_{K\subseteq U\ { m compact}} \operatorname{fib}\bigl(F(Y)\to F(Y\setminus K)\bigr). \tag{D.8} \] For a continuous map $f:X\to Y$ between such spaces, cosheaf pushforward $f_+$ is $(f_+G)(U)=G(f^{-1}U)$. The topological operation with proper support is $f_!=\mathbb V_Y^{-1}f_+\mathbb V_X$ and has a right adjoint $f^!$. For proper $f$ it agrees with $f_*$. This does not identify $f_!$ with the left adjoint $f_\sharp$ of D.7. | claim (return: Known) | Unverified citation (HA 5.5.5.1; Volpe 6.9). |

matches.text: | BISITE D.11 | The realization comparison for every proper map of finite posets. Let $f:P\to Q$ be a $W_\infty$-proper map of finite posets. Equivalently, for every $p\in P$ and $q\geq f(p)$ the outgoing lifting poset \[ L(p,q)=\{r\in P:r\geq p,\ f(r)=q\} \tag{D.11a} \] is weakly contractible. This holds for spaces, spectra, and the derived category of modules over any ring. matches.text: | BISITE D.13 | A specified stable cosheaf counterpart for smooth finite-poset maps. There is a precise geometric dual on finite coefficients which uses the maximum stratification and Verdier transport. Let $\mathcal C$ be spectra or modules over a commutative ring, let $D$ be the coefficient duality on finite spectra or perfect modules, and let $E_P^{\max}:\operatorname{Fun}(P,\mathcal C)\to \operatorname{Shv}(\|NP\|;\mathcal C)$ be G.10 for $P^{\mathrm{op}}$. Define the contravariant fully faithful functor \[ \Phi_P(F)=\mathbb V_{\|NP\|}\,E_P^{\max}(DF), \qquad F\in\operatorname{Fun}(P^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal C^{\mathrm{perf}}). \tag{D.13a} \] If $f:P\to Q$ is categorically smooth, then its realization $g$ satisfies \[ \Phi_Q(f_!F)\simeq g_+\Phi_P(F). \tag{D.13b} \] Thus ordinary cosheaf pushforward realizes this specified dual of left Kan extension. The cosheaf subcategories in (D.13a) are defined as Verdier images of maximum-constructible perfect sheaves; they are not being identified with literal minimum-constructible cosheaves. For a noncommutative ring the target coefficients are modules over its opposite ring. | claim (return: Proved) | Unverified. |

matches.text: | RESIDUE H.7 | The program \path{code/GHIJ/finite_poset_direct_image.py} independently enumerates all maps between one representative of every poset isomorphism class with at most five objects, including the empty poset. The counts of posets of sizes $0,1,2,3,4,5$ are $1,1,2,5,16,63$. It examines $1,349,916$ monotone maps and recognizes $96,372$ proper maps. Properness is certified by explicit simplicial collapses of every nonempty outgoing lifting order complex; noncontractible cases are rejected by homology over $\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb F_2$. The program aborts rather than classifying an acyclic but uncertified complex as contractible. No such undecided case occurs in this range. For every proper map and every nonempty target simplex, it computes the categorical stalk and the actual geometric-fibre cellular cohomology, for the constant coefficient and for each principal-cosieve indicator. This gives $5,536,094$ stalk/coefficient cases, each computed over both $\mathbb Q$ and $\mathbb F_2$, with no discrepancy. A fibre cell is indexed by a source chain meeting each level of the target simplex; it is a product of simplices, of dimension $\|\kappa\|-\|\sigma\|$. Its signed boundary deletes one vertex while keeping every level nonempty, using the product-boundary sign. The code verifies that consecutive boundary matrices multiply to zero. Exact rational ranks use integer elimination with gcd reduction, and binary ranks use bit arithmetic. For a principal cosieve, extension from the corresponding closed subcomplex reduces both computations to its intersection with the relevant fibre or lower inverse image. The supplied per-map CSV records all tests as successful; the JSON gives the totals by source and target size. These numerical comparisons check cohomology, not a replacement proof of the canonical mate; the latter is established in H.1. | claim (return: Proved) | no review |

matches.text: The claim that the “donnée … est équivalente” to compatible subsets of $\pi_0(D_d)$ makes the admissible closed $\Sigma$ recoverable from the global component data rather than arbitrary local labels. This **adds** a closed-subset classification to the branch-labeling torsors of `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 109 and 117, where permutation monodromy is already built into the flag spaces. matches.text: The description “c’est donc un crible” claims that the selected analytic subcategory is full and closed under every arrow whose target lies in it. This **restates** the source/target and composition formalism of `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 113–114, but **adds** the equivalence of such componentwise subcategories with admissible closed subsets. The direction of closure is essential: (250) selects arrows by their targets, and (251) ensures that their sources are also selected, so every surviving flag is determined by its final object together with its incoming chain. The equivalence should therefore be read with the analytic and component-selection conditions retained, rather than as a classification by arbitrary abstract subcategories of the incidence category.

It **restates** the cospan and hole-filling construction in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 162 and 168, with the closed-point groupoids now discrete. matches.text: The desired “vue d’ensemble” can be organized by composing group homomorphisms over the arithmetic quotient, with residue-field maps supplied by decomposition groups rather than by nonexistent canonical inclusions $k(s)\subset K$. This adds a comparison between the local groupoid in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 26, and the conjugacy classification of splittings on scan 63 (“mod. autom. intérieurs”). For a fixed based extension, a splitting gives an actual conjugation action on its geometric kernel, whereas changing the base point or transport path changes the comparison by an inner automorphism. The latter dependence is explicit in SGA 1, Exposé XIII, §2.10, and explains why the author’s insistence on “effectives” requires compatible choices (Grothendieck, 1971/2003).

matches.text: The suggestion of a criterion “sur les groupes $p$-divisibles” is appropriate to abelian-variety data, but the Jacobian’s Barsotti–Tate group alone cannot detect every node of the curve. The compact-type construction in RN100-03 also works over a suitable mixed-characteristic trait: its Jacobian is an abelian scheme although its curve is singular, reflecting the distinction $g=\sum g_\alpha+h_1$ in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 12 (Deligne & Mumford, 1969). A genuinely nonabelian replacement is available for smooth proper curves of genus at least two with a regular semistable model and an integral base point over a complete characteristic-zero DVR with perfect residue field of characteristic $p$: good reduction is equivalent to crystallinity of the unipotent $p$-adic étale fundamental group (Andreatta et al., 2015, Theorems 1.6 and 1.9). This differs from testing only the Jacobian’s $p$-divisible group and should remain separate from the prime-to-$p$ outer-inertia criterion.

matches.text: The second version asserts that the semisimplicial family of germ topoi has colimit “équivalente canoniquement” to $V^*_{\Sigma,X}$, but gives no descent proof. It **adds** a general admissible-support gluing statement to the nonformal neighborhood structure anticipated in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 133, and must be distinguished from the two different gluing constructions in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 163–166. A proof should define the comparison pseudodiagram and establish effective descent for its local branch charts, including the relevant comparison $2$-cells. Lurie’s Theorem 6.1.3.9 and Proposition 6.1.3.10 give a possible modern descent test for diagrams inside an infinity-topos, but do not identify this colimit of varying germ topoi without an additional construction (Lurie, 2009, pp. 548–549 in the updated author PDF).

matches.text: The phrase “c’est donc un crible” suggests checking admissible supports and all selected flags by finite incidence calculations in a branch chart, then imposing invariance under branch transport. This proposal **adds** a computational use to the Boolean branch poset and its permutation torsor in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 106, 109, and 116: choose local intersections, close the selection under incoming arrows, and retain precisely the flags whose final vertex is selected. Confidence is high for the finite local calculation because the branch poset and the closure rule are explicit; confidence in a global implementation is conditional on correctly retaining monodromy and the analytic component data. This is a suggested consistency check and construction procedure, not a claim of novelty or a proof of the topos gluing theorem.

matches.text: The assertion expressing “$\Pi_1(X)$ … comme somme amalgamée” is the curve case of gluing the complement to genuine neighborhoods of the missing points. It **restates** the cospan and hole-filling construction in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 162 and 168, with the closed-point groupoids now discrete. For an actual open tubular-neighborhood cover, Brown’s Theorem 3.4 proves the fundamental-groupoid pushout using an object set meeting every component of the overlap, so disconnected punctured neighborhoods cause no problem (Brown, 1967, pp. 391–392). Passage from those actual neighborhoods to the manuscript’s germ topoi still requires the relevant fundamental-groupoid comparison; the theorem does not assert an equivalence of topoi.

matches.text: The admission that the reduction “ne s’explicite pas aisément, au niveau des groupoïdes fondamentaux” concerns information lost when passing from a closed immersion of topoi to its induced groupoid map. It **restates** the distinction between the mixed recollement topos and its multigaloisian reflection in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 163–166, and **adds** the concrete problem of recovering open complements from that reduced data. A simple illustration is that both pairs $(\mathbb C,\{0\})$ and $(\mathbb C,\mathbb C)$ induce, up to equivalence, the same arrow of trivial connected fundamental groupoids, while their open complements have respectively fundamental group $\mathbb Z$ and no objects. This illustration concerns the bare groupoid arrow, and scan 180 supplies a separate warning about higher cohomology lost by a proposed constructible reconstruction; neither warning identifies the comparison in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 167, with the one refuted on 180.

matches.text: The proposal to discard repeated indices uses the fact that “les op. … de dégénérescence sont des iso.” It **restates** the isomorphisms and criticism of nonstrict indexing in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 134–135, and **adds** a systematic restriction to strictly decreasing flags. A rigorous implementation should compare the complete diagrams, including repeated face maps, rather than infer preservation of a colimit from objectwise isomorphisms alone. Lurie’s cofinality criterion offers a precise test once the comparison of indexing categories has been constructed, with contractibility of the relevant comma categories still to be verified here (Lurie, 2009, Theorem 4.1.3.1, p. 236 in the updated author PDF).

Treumann’s exit-path classifications supply comparison targets under conical-stratification and tameness hypotheses; identifying these germ flags with exit paths remains a separate task (Treumann, 2009, Theorems 1.2 and 7.14). matches.text: The “contre-exemple type” shows that the indicated constructible-sheaf topos on $S^2=\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$ has the single-arrow description while the sphere retains positive-dimensional cohomology, and ends by asking how to understand the homotopy type of a topos obtained by “recollement”. 180-02 — Homotopy pushout versus ordinary groupoid colimit

matches.text: For the displayed span $\{1\}\leftarrow\mathbb Z\to\{1\}$, compare the colimit in groupoids with the homotopy pushout after applying classifying spaces: the latter is $*\cup^h_{B\mathbb Z}*\simeq\Sigma S^1\simeq S^2$, while the former has trivial fundamental groupoid. This **adds** a higher-homotopy diagnostic to the essentially commuting groupoid amalgamated sum of `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 166, and to the normal-closure calculation of its fundamental group in scans 168–169. Confidence is high because the suspension is the explicit double-mapping-cylinder model of this span, but identifying that model with any particular manuscript topos still requires a comparison theorem. Thus the source's “on ne reconstitue pas” must not be paraphrased as saying that the displayed groupoid diagram cannot support a construction recovering the sphere.

matches.text: The margin “dans le contexte des VA” plausibly alludes to the abelian-variety good-reduction criterion, but neither the abbreviation nor this autobiographical claim identifies a particular publication. Its terminology restates the use of “V.A.” and $\pi_{\mathrm{ab}}$ in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 64, but that passage concerns recognizing points and does not establish a curve-reduction theorem. The Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich–Serre–Tate criterion detects good reduction of an abelian variety from its prime-to-residue-characteristic Tate module; the precise statement was checked in Andreatta et al. (2015, Theorem 1.1), with Serre and Tate (1968) retained as the original bibliographic reference. For a proper curve this controls its Jacobian, and the compact-type example below prevents transferring the criterion to the curve itself.

matches.text: The expectation “être connu sur $H_1$” invites the following editorial counterexample: join two elliptic curves over $\mathbf Q$ at rational points and smooth their single node over $\mathbf Q[[t]]$, locally by $xy=t$. This adds a reduction test to `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 12, whose formula $g=\sum g_\alpha+h_1$ separates the component genera from cycles in the dual graph. The graph is a tree, so the degree-zero Picard scheme has no toric part and the Jacobian has good reduction, whereas uniqueness of the stable model leaves the genus-two curve with its singular special fiber; its inertia on $H_1$ is therefore trivial despite bad curve reduction (Deligne & Mumford, 1969, Proposition 1.5, Theorem 1.11, Lemma 1.17, and Theorem 2.5; Grothendieck, 1971/2003, Exposé X, Corollary 3.9). Confidence is high because independent node smoothing, the graph–torus computation, and stable-model uniqueness give each step; removing one section through a smooth rational point leaves $H_1$ unchanged and gives an affine hyperbolic counterexample as well.

matches.text: At scan 115, manuscript page 57, the final paragraph says that the quotient of $\mathcal E_L^{\overline L}$ “ne … dépend pas du modèle $X$ choisi”, for $X$ proper and regular. This **adds** a birationally invariant quotient to the local curve-boundary construction in **LM_140-2_text.tex, scans 25–28**. Given two such models, a finite étale cover of one is unramified at every $K$-valuation by the valuative criterion of properness, hence at the codimension-one local rings of the other, and its finite normalization over the other is étale by regular-target purity; thus the quotient of the fixed $G_L$, not merely its abstract isomorphism type, agrees (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tags 0BQJ and 0BMB). Confidence: high when the proper regular models exist; this comparison does not itself prove their existence or require a general resolution theorem to compare two already given models.

matches.text: At scan 119, manuscript page 59, (30) begins $N_{x'}\simeq\mathcal E_{\widetilde U_x}^{\overline L}$, and the preceding paragraph makes the effective map depend on a geometric point and a path or field embedding. This **restates** the pointed henselian-trait construction of **LM_140-2_text.tex, scans 25–26**, while making the conjugacy choices explicit. The fixed fields of decomposition and inertia are respectively the fraction fields of the henselization and strict henselization, so fixing the prolongation $x'$ gives the asserted embedded subgroups, whereas forgetting it leaves conjugacy classes (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 58.13.1, Tag 0BSW). Confidence: high; independence of a model means dependence only on the valuation and these choices, not a choice-free embedding into $G_L$.

This **adds** a quotient presentation to **LM_140-2_text.tex, scans 26–28**, where the local inertia maps are attached to an already specified curve and boundary. For regular integral finite-type $U/K$, every centered valuation's inertia dies on finite étale covers, while the codimension-one inertia already generates the kernel by finite normalization and regular-target purity (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tags 0BTD and 0BMB). matches.text: At scan 122, the second paragraph begins “Sauf erreur” and claims that the codimension-zero and codimension-one points are the only ones whose local ring “soit noethérien”. The example and consequence in **130-O1–130-O2** give a valuation ring of $\mathbf Q(x,y)$ with value group $\mathbf Z$ and residue field $\mathbf Q$, hence a noetherian DVR at a point of manuscript codimension two, contradicting this assertion. This **differs** from the divisorial curve-local “jauge” in **LM_140-2_text.tex, scan 25**: being a DVR is a valuation-theoretic property, whereas being divisorial imposes the additional residue-transcendence condition (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 10.50.18, Tag 00I8). Confidence: high because the explicit value group and residue field determine both sides of the contradiction; the counterexample is cross-referenced rather than proved twice.

matches.text: For each $h\in L^\times$, take the closure of the graph of the rational map $X\dashrightarrow\mathbf P^1_K$ defined by $h$, and normalize it, obtaining another proper normal model of $L/K$. At the compatible center on this model, one of the two standard charts of $\mathbf P^1$ makes $h$ or $h^{-1}$ regular, which proves the valuation property without using resolution of singularities. This supplies a completion of the manuscript argument and adds an inverse-system construction to `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 75–77; compare Temkin (2011, Lemma 2.2.2) and the element-or-inverse criterion in The Stacks Project Authors (n.d., Tag 00I8, Lemma 10.50.5). Confidence: high for the unrestricted proper normal-model category, because the graph construction is proper birational and the two-chart alternative is exhaustive; a restricted indexing category requires a separate cofinality check.

matches.text: As a test of the general indexing, let $D_1,D_2\subset\mathbf P^1\times\mathbf P^1$ be the diagonal and the graph of $z\mapsto2z$; they meet transversely at two points. This adds a component-counting diagnostic to `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 128–129, whose flag spaces retain component data, and to the componentwise correction on 135. matches.text: The question « quelle est sa signification topologique? » suggests replacing the bare incidence complex by a diagram carrying the fundamental groupoids of strata, the local lattices of branches, and the normal torus torsors, before taking any homotopy colimit. **Context comparison — adds:** `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 121–123 and 128–133, already supplies the lattices, torsors, flags, and the distinction between the undecorated and decorated groupoids; cote 149 adds the arithmetic maps into the fundamental group of the complement. For fine saturated log schemes locally of finite type over $\mathbf C$, Carchedi et al. (2017, introduction and Theorem 6.4) compare the Kato–Nakayama space and the infinite root stack after profinite completion, including torus fibers whose ranks follow the strata. **Our confidence: medium**, because these fibers match the manuscript’s local ingredients, whereas identifying its particular formal or étale object $U_\infty$ with the appropriate boundary of that construction still requires a comparison theorem and cannot follow from the incidence complex alone.

matches.text: The parenthetical “défini à iso unique près ?...” asks for a uniqueness statement about the neighborhood germ, and the sentence about descent to multiplicities is still exploratory. This adds an immersion-relative construction to the germ around an actual subset defined by its neighborhood filter in `LM_140-4_text.tex`, scan 245, and to the filter-based category of germs on scan 242. A proof needs a stated category of germs over $Y$ and an account of local branch separation: uniqueness over the ambient object is a different assertion from uniqueness of a bare germ or of a chosen tubular parametrization.

matches.text: The desired “vue d’ensemble” can be organized by composing group homomorphisms over the arithmetic quotient, with residue-field maps supplied by decomposition groups rather than by nonexistent canonical inclusions $k(s)\subset K$. This adds a comparison between the local groupoid in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 26, and the conjugacy classification of splittings on scan 63 (“mod. autom. intérieurs”). For a fixed based extension, a splitting gives an actual conjugation action on its geometric kernel, whereas changing the base point or transport path changes the comparison by an inner automorphism. The latter dependence is explicit in SGA 1, Exposé XIII, §2.10, and explains why the author’s insistence on “effectives” requires compatible choices (Grothendieck, 1971/2003).

matches.text: The expectation “être connu sur $H_1$” invites the following editorial counterexample: join two elliptic curves over $\mathbf Q$ at rational points and smooth their single node over $\mathbf Q[[t]]$, locally by $xy=t$. This adds a reduction test to `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 12, whose formula $g=\sum g_\alpha+h_1$ separates the component genera from cycles in the dual graph. The graph is a tree, so the degree-zero Picard scheme has no toric part and the Jacobian has good reduction, whereas uniqueness of the stable model leaves the genus-two curve with its singular special fiber; its inertia on $H_1$ is therefore trivial despite bad curve reduction (Deligne & Mumford, 1969, Proposition 1.5, Theorem 1.11, Lemma 1.17, and Theorem 2.5; Grothendieck, 1971/2003, Exposé X, Corollary 3.9). Confidence is high because independent node smoothing, the graph–torus computation, and stable-model uniqueness give each step; removing one section through a smooth rational point leaves $H_1$ unchanged and gives an affine hyperbolic counterexample as well.

This restates the realization meaning of “action ext. admissible” in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 410, but does not force a realizing curve to be the literal special fiber of the given model. The ramified quadratic-twist calculation in RN103-03–RN103-04 supplies a different realizing curve over the residue field and therefore refutes that inference in the stated generality. The Tate-cusp calculation in RN103-05 gives a separate case where geometric realization really is obstructed, so bad reduction alone does not decide this question.

matches.text: The question “qu’attendre d’une telle action ?” can first be separated into its formal and geometric parts. It restates the splitting framework of `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 63, while scan 413 adds an independent admissibility condition for actual lifts. After fixing one section $s$, another has the form $s^{\prime}(g)=c(g)s(g)$ with $c$ a continuous nonabelian $1$-cocycle in $\pi$, and its action is $\operatorname{Int}(c(g))\alpha_s(g)$. Thus changing the section of (31) preserves the outer action but can change the actual action and its point-theoretic interpretation; this is a direct calculation from multiplication in the extension.

This restates the “maquette” in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 11, and adds an arithmetic question to the three boundary partitions of the four-pointed line on scan 61. Independent node-smoothing parameters give local boundary directions, while the graph distinguishes a separating node from a loop contributing to the Jacobian’s toric part (Deligne & Mumford, 1969, Proposition 1.5 and Lemma 1.17). Our mixed-characteristic check is the good pair $\mathbf P^1_{\mathbf Q_p}\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}$, whose $p$-adic homology $\mathbf Z_p(1)^2$ is ramified although its prime-to-$p$ homology is unramified, so an all-primes reading of c) cannot be equated with d) in the later $p$-adic parenthesis (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tag 03PK). Confidence is high because the two Kummer generators give these cyclotomic modules directly; in the original residue-characteristic-zero setting, RN100-03 and RN103-01 separately disprove d)$\Rightarrow$a).

matches.text: The suggestion of a criterion “sur les groupes $p$-divisibles” is appropriate to abelian-variety data, but the Jacobian’s Barsotti–Tate group alone cannot detect every node of the curve. The compact-type construction in RN100-03 also works over a suitable mixed-characteristic trait: its Jacobian is an abelian scheme although its curve is singular, reflecting the distinction $g=\sum g_\alpha+h_1$ in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 12 (Deligne & Mumford, 1969). A genuinely nonabelian replacement is available for smooth proper curves of genus at least two with a regular semistable model and an integral base point over a complete characteristic-zero DVR with perfect residue field of characteristic $p$: good reduction is equivalent to crystallinity of the unipotent $p$-adic étale fundamental group (Andreatta et al., 2015, Theorems 1.6 and 1.9). This differs from testing only the Jacobian’s $p$-divisible group and should remain separate from the prime-to-$p$ outer-inertia criterion.

matches.text: The margin’s “n'est pas étale” concerns integral separation of boundary points, a property stronger than their rationality over the generic field. This differs from `LM_140-4_text.tex`, scan 150, where the generalized-Jacobian description begins with a boundary already “étale de degré $3$”. In RN103-01, all punctures are rational and their boundary permutation module is constant, yet their closures collide; the abelianized representation consequently loses the cross-ratio degeneration. The proposed genus-zero investigation therefore isolates precisely why a boundary permutation representation, even together with the compactification’s homology, need not recover good reduction of the pointed curve.

This differs from `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 413, which explicitly anticipates “pathologiques” among lifts of an admissible outer action and treats actual admissibility as an additional condition. The quadratic-twist example supplies geometric outer and actual actions at bad reduction, whereas the Tate example supplies a nongeometric outer action, so neither alone realizes the combination sought here. Constructing that combination would require controlling the section cocycle while retaining a fixed geometric outer action, the separate problem isolated in RN101-03.

matches.text: At scan 106, display (4) and its following sentence, “la clôture alg. de $k(x)$ dans $\Omega$” accompanies a canonical comparison whose first subscript remains $\alpha$ or $X$. This **adds** a larger separably closed field of a base point to **LM_140-2_text.tex, scan 22**, which describes a separable residue-field closure, and scan 108 of the present manuscript itself explicitly says “clôtures séparables dans $\Omega$”. Finite étale residue extensions factor through the separable algebraic closure inside $\Omega$, giving the fibre-functor comparison for the fixed scheme $X$ (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 58.6.3, Tag 0BQ8), but a merely separably closed $\Omega$ need not contain an algebraic closure in the purely inseparable sense. Confidence: high in this distinction, medium in the intended terminology, and low in the marked subscript; it does not assert invariance of $\pi_1(X_\Omega)$ under changing the base field of $X$.

matches.text: At scan 107, manuscript page 53, the parenthesis before (7), “plus gén. $\mathcal E_Y^Z$ chaque fois qu'on a un $Y$-schéma $Z$ $1$-connexe”, proposes a fibre functor based on $Z$. This **adds** a scheme over $Y$ to the representing-object formulation in **LM_140-2_text.tex, scan 8, Proposition 1.5**, and to its pointed-cover formulation in scans 9–10. For finite étale covers, the construction is precise when $Z$ is nonempty and connected with trivial étale fundamental group: send a cover $W\to Y$ to $\pi_0(W\times_Y Z)$, since every such pullback is a finite disjoint union of copies of $Z$, and use Galois-category reconstruction for its automorphism group (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Tags 0BMQ and 0BQ8). Confidence: high for this finite-étale formulation; extending the same wording to all locally constant objects requires retaining the context's separate hypotheses on the topos.

matches.text: At scan 110, after (13), “Cette hypothèse sera tjrs satisfaite si $Y=\operatorname{Spec}K$ … si $X$ est géom. $0$-connexe” **restates** the arithmetic/geometric extension framework of **LM_140-2_text.tex, scans 22 and 47**, while (12) **adds** identification with the group of $X_T$. The arithmetic statement is valid for a quasi-compact, quasi-separated $X/K$ with connected geometric fibre: $1\to\pi_1(X_{\bar K})\to\pi_1(X)\to G_K\to 1$ (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 58.14.3, Tag 0BTX). It does not justify the stronger assertion for every simply connected $T$, and unrestricted field extension of a nonproper scheme in characteristic $p$ already supplies a counterexample, detailed in 110-O1 (Landesman, 2024, Example 1.7). Confidence: high in the arithmetic theorem and in the distinction between it and the unrestricted reading of (12).

matches.text: At scan 111, manuscript page 55, (14)–(16) assert a “factorisation can.” with $Y'$ “étale fini ou pro-étale fini” and explicitly replace $X\times_YT$ by $X\times_{Y'}T$. This **adds** a relative component factor to **LM_140-2_text.tex, scan 83**, where a finite base extension separates geometric connected components and makes the relevant images over the base Galois group explicit. A precise finite case is the Stein factorization of a proper flat finitely presented map with geometrically reduced fibres, for which $Y'\to Y$ is finite étale (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 58.15.1, Tag 0BUN); the closed image of $\pi_1(X)\to\pi_1(Y)$ instead determines a pointed profinite cover in Galois theory, without automatically being an open subgroup or a finite cover. Confidence: high in these two constructions, with the fibre identification still subject to the exactness qualifications in 109-Q1.

matches.text: At scan 116, immediately before (21), “Si $U$ est un modèle quelconque; il se plonge dans un $X$” inherits the proper regular $X$ of scan 115. This **differs** in scope from **LM_140-2_text.tex, scans 19 and 25**, where the ambient curve is already projective and smooth. Nagata compactification supplies a proper compactification for a separated finite-type $U/K$, but gives no regularity conclusion; a singular $U$ cannot be an open subscheme of a regular $X$, and even for regular $U$ a regular compactification is an additional existence input (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Theorem 38.33.8, Tag 0F41). Confidence: high in the missing qualification; the ensuing quotient calculation is sound for an actual dense open $U\subset X$ with $X$ regular, and must not be used as an argument for unrestricted resolution of singularities.

The claim **restates** the characteristic-zero Kummer kernel of **LM_140-2_text.tex, scan 26**, and its explicit local Tate-system formulation in scan 125. matches.text: At the end of scan 121, manuscript page 60, “ce n'est pas un schéma !” is qualified by the insertion “si $n\geq2$”, and scan 122 adds that $n=0,1$ are the only scheme cases. For a finitely generated field extension $L/K$, the zero-dimensional space is $\operatorname{Spec}L$, and in transcendence degree one the normal proper curve already represents the valuation space; in higher transcendence degree, 121-O1 supplies a separate obstruction to any affine open neighborhood. This **differs** from the affine-transition limit in **LM_140-4_text.tex, scans 23–24**, and is compatible with Olberding's criterion relating affine subspaces of a Zariski–Riemann space to Prüfer intersection rings (Olberding, 2015, Proposition 6.1; preprint Theorem 6.1). Confidence: high under this normal finite-type model interpretation; neither the mere existence of nonnoetherian stalks nor the incorrect noetherian-stalk assertion assessed in 122-CJ1 would prove nonschematicity.

This **adds** a relative birational space over a general base to the local curve-trait construction in **LM_140-2_text.tex, scan 25**. For an integral base one may use its proper birational modifications and valuations of its function field with centers on it; Temkin's relative construction goes further, using separated morphisms of quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes, without an excellence requirement, and its general stalk description uses semivaluation rings rather than necessarily valuation rings of one field (Temkin, 2011, Sections 1.1 and 2.1–2.2). Confidence: high in this precise modern continuation, with the modification category and integral versus general relative setting made explicit rather than inferred from the short margin.

Both maps to the inertia of the crossing $(0,0)$ have Kummer weights $(1,2)$, hence give the same image conjugacy class in the fixed product $U=(\mathbf P^1\setminus\{0,1,\infty\})^2$, as computed in 130-O3. This adds a failure of injectivity for valuation images on one model to `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 117–118, and differs from separating distinct curve cusps because both valuations have the same boundary center. matches.text: The transvection example can be checked directly if the uncertain upper-right matrix entry is the retained first reading $1$: the generator acts by $(x,y)\mapsto(x+y,y)$ and fixes the line $y=0$. An equivariant linear section of the quotient would send $1$ to a vector $(a,1)$ fixed by the generator, but that vector is sent to $(a+1,1)$, so the tangent extension does not split and an equivariant tubular diffeomorphism inducing the prescribed normal identification cannot exist. This adds an explicit verification to the proposed descent in `LM_140-4_text.tex`, scans 259–260, where local coordinates have no such equivariance constraint; confidence is high conditional on the entry $1$, and the calculation is a test of the author's example rather than a claim of novelty.

The proposal adds a conditional repair to the quotient-germ programme of `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 78–80, and to the equivariance comparisons in `LM_140-4_text.tex`, scans 263–264; confidence is high for the metric construction under the stated hypotheses, but it does not establish descent for arbitrary multiplicities or simultaneous compatibility with every boundary branch.
